title: MA8-09524
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The principal claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXXX, his spouse, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXXX, and their four children, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, both minors, and XXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXXX, who are of the age of majority, are all citizens of Mexico. Mr. XXXXX XXXX and his family all allege that they are "Convention refugees" and "persons in need of protection" under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The father, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXXX, is the designated representative for his two minor sons, XXXX and XXXX.

The principal claimant alleged that he was XXXXXXXX Mexico City. He had a variety of problems because of individuals whose names he does not know who were dealing drugs on his street. He knows their nicknames, XX XXXX and XX XXXX, but does not have a good relationship with these neighbours.

He returned from work on XXXX, 2008, and found these people selling drugs in front of his house. He asked them to leave, but they did not cooperate. Given that they live 50 metres from his home, the claimant insisted that they leave. Voices were raised and a fist fight ensued, but neighbours and the children arrived and made them leave.

He did not file a complaint against them because they often threatened people in the neighbourhood. Furthermore, a neighbour, XXXX, had problems with them and he disappeared in XXXX 2007. He was found dead one month later.
The next day, XXXX, 2008, the claimant and his parents went to see them to ask them to behave responsibly. The two individuals refused and threatened to kill them if they filed a complaint.

At about 10:30 p.m. on XXXX, 2008, the situation became more dangerous. The claimant returned from work XXXXXX and they blocked the driveway. They started arguing again. One hour later, one of them rang his doorbell and asked him to step outside. The claimant refused, and the man told him that they were fed up with him and they were going to kill him because he was interfering with their business. The claimant and his son XXXX tried to restrain him, but the man broke loose and ran toward the street. They were unable to catch him because he climbed into a XXXX XXXXXX and fired some shots at them as he left. They were not hit.
They did not file a complaint because they were scared and they knew that the police cooperates with them, because they are their clients and they receive payments to let them continue.
They therefore decided to leave the country on XXXX, 2008.
After analyzing the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel is of the opinion that the claimants are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection." ANALYSIS Identity

In light of the documents submitted as evidence for XXXXX XXXXX XXXXXX, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXXX, XXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXXX, namely photocopies of the four passports, valid from XXXX, 2008, to XXXX, 2011, the panel is satisfied as to the identity of these four claimants.

In addition, XXXX XXXXX submitted as evidence the photocopies of his passport, which is valid from XXXX, 2008, to XXXX, 2011, and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXXX submitted the photocopies of his passport, which is valid from XXXX, 2008, until XXXX, 2011. The panel is therefore satisfied as to the identity of these two claimants. Credibility
The principal claimant is not credible, because of omissions and major contradictions that appeared during his testimony.

During his testimony, the claimant stated that three incidents occurred, specifically on XXXXX and XX, 2008, and on XXXX, 2008. So the panel asked him to recount what took place during those incidents.

The claimant stated that when he arrived home on XXXX, 2008, the two drug dealers that he fears, XX XXXX and XX XXXX, forced him out of his car and hit him. Surprised, the panel asked how they made him get out of a car and he replied that they opened it, grabbed him and brought him out. The panel points out that he wrote in his narrative1 that, during this incident, he went to see them to tell them to go elsewhere to conduct their business. The claimant then stated that he drove towards them and that they then got him out and hit him.

The panel does not accept this explanation, because the claimant describes this event in two paragraphs2 and at no time is it mentioned that the claimant got out of a vehicle that day. He states, on the contrary, that they got into a fist fight, which implies that they certainly were not in a vehicle, but were outside, since it would be difficult to have a fist fight in a vehicle.

The panel does not believe that the incident of XXXXX took place, since he contradicted himself in describing the circumstances-that he was in a vehicle and that he was walking-and this undermines his credibility.

The claimant recounted that, on the day after the incident of XXXXX, 2008, he and his parents went to see these two men at their home. He explained that it was in the hopes of having a discussion, of putting an end to this problem. However, instead of talking, they insulted them and told them not to file a complaint. A little later, the panel asked him how he had been insulted and he explained that they swore at them loudly. On that topic, the panel asked whether, on XXXXX, these men had said anything else to him, and he replied [translation] "not that I remember" and added that he did not remember. The panel noted that it is stated in his narrative that he received death threats on that day,3 and the claimant stated emphatically that he did not receive death threats, which surprised the panel. The panel pointed out that he also mentions in his narrative that a member of the family would pay very dearly for it. The claimant stated that no, the threats were against him. He added, as if to correct himself, that, if there were threats, they were against him; and that if there were death threats, it would be the same as making them against the family.

Later, after a break, counsel again questioned the claimant on this topic, implying that the claimant first stated that he had received such threats and then stated that he had not. The claimant then explained that he might have misunderstood the question at that point.

The panel does not believe that the claimant went to the home of these two drug dealers, first of all, because his reasons for doing so are not very clear and, secondly, because he alleged that he went there with his parents, including his mother. The panel asked him why he went with his parents and he replied that it was to have a discussion. The panel does not believe that they accompanied him because this would be putting them at risk, and more importantly, because he does not mention in his narrative that they accompanied him. Moreover, the claimant clearly stated that he did not receive such threats and then he tried to adjust his testimony after the break, when he was questioned by his counsel. He then alleged that he had not understood the question, when, in fact, the claimant had repeated the sentence and stated that the threats were against him, which implies that he was well aware that they were talking about threats.

In light of this omission, the visits with his parents, and particularly the contradiction regarding the threats that he did or did not receive, the panel does not believe that the incident of XXXXX took place, which undermines his credibility.

Regarding the incident of XXXXX, there is a contradiction between the principal claimant's statement and that of his eldest son XXXXX. When the panel asked the father to recount the event, he explained that someone rang their doorbell after eleven o'clock and asked him to step outside. He allegedly refused, stating that it was out of the question, and his son XXXXX allegedly went out. The panel asked him whether the man was alone, and the claimant replied that he was and that he came right up to the house. The panel asked XXXXX why he had told the immigration officer upon his arrival4 that two men came to his house looking for his father. XXXXX explained that, initially, there was one man and that later there were two men.

The panel does not accept this explanation since, in the same statement, XXXXX went on to tell the immigration officer5 that there was a lively discussion between them and his father. The use of the word [translation] "them" implies that there was more than one person. He then stated that he went out. That is why the panel is of the opinion that there is a contradiction between the father's contention that one person rang their doorbell and the son's statement that two people came to his house. Furthermore, XXXXX is attempting to adjust his testimony, given that he told the immigration officer that some men came to his house and then, when confronted, he stated that he initially saw one person and then two. This undermines his credibility.

This contradiction between the statements made by the father and those made by the son undermines their credibility and, consequently, the panel does not believe that the incident of XXXXX took place.

Because of these omissions and contradictions, the panel does not believe that the events of XXXXX and XX and of XXXXX took place and, consequently, the panel does not believe that the claimants were threatened by drug dealers as alleged.

A strange event happened after the claimants had been in Canada for two years. The principal claimant's brother, XXXX, was murdered on XXXX, 2010, almost two years after their departure on XXXX, 2008. A number of exhibits were submitted regarding this death,6 and the panel believes that the claimant's brother, XXXX XXXXX XXXXXX, is deceased, even though some of the exhibits contain errors, such as XXXX name being confused with that of XXXX, another brother.7

The principal claimant alleged that this brother died because someone living across the street from the home that they shared with their mother killed XXXX out of vengeance. The claimant added that his brother XXXX was murdered because he and XXXX had had a number of problems with drug dealers. The claimant's mother sent her son a copy of the statement that she gave to police8 and a little later, of the addendum that she made to her statement.9 In her statement to the police, she explains that her son was killed because of a disagreement that he had on XXXXX, 2010, with a man named XXXXX. This man lived across from her. His wife asked her son XXXX to stop this man, her husband, from throwing his daughter off the balcony. This man, XXXXX, then allegedly told XXXX that he was going to kill him because he, himself, was a member of a gang.

The panel asked the claimant about the fact that, in her statement to the police,10 his mother states that his brother XXXX had a police record for theft and that he served time in a penitentiary. The claimant stated that, in fact, that must have happened the year before he died. The panel asked him how much time he spent in prison and the claimant tried to play down that fact by stating that the incident was not a big deal and that he must have spent barely a day there. The panel reiterated that his mother wrote that he spent time in a penitentiary and that it was surely more than one day. The claimant clearly did not want to discuss it any further.

Given that the claimant stated at the hearing that his brother XXXX lived near him, that his spouse described their neighbourhood as being unsafe and that even the newspaper describes the streets in that neighbourhood11 as [translation] "dark and dangerous neighbourhood streets," the panel has doubts as to the reasons behind the claimant's brother's murder. The panel believes that this brother was killed, based on the exhibits submitted. However, the panel is of the opinion that the mother's story claiming that XXXX was killed because he tried to help a neighbour is rather far-fetched, since the panel has difficulty believing that someone could be killed for such a minor reason.

The panel believes, rather, that XXXX murder was a settling of accounts, as mentioned in one of the exhibits,12 a newspaper article that discusses the possibility that this man's death could be explained as a settling of accounts. In fact, this murder took place almost two years after the claimant's departure, and he never mentioned that his brother had the same problems as he did before learning of his death. He only mentions it in the exhibit submitted on February 3, 2011,13 a few days before the hearing, in which he states that [translation] "My brother and I had many problems with drug dealers...to the point that they threatened to kill us." Furthermore, this brother was incarcerated for a crime the previous year, and the claimant does not want to explain the reasons for this incarceration. His reluctance surprised the panel. Counsel later alleged that the expression [translation] "settling of accounts" is a very vague expression that could indicate a problem in the neighbourhood just as well as problem with organized crime. However, the panel is of the opinion that the use of this expression in a newspaper article, under the circumstances described-namely that he died from gunshot wounds and was shot three times-indicates that it is very unlikely that this was simply a dispute between neighbours, but that it was actually a settling of accounts related to organized crime.

To be certain that this death was not related to the motives alleged by the claimant, the panel asked him about the connection between this death and the men who allegedly attacked the claimant. The claimant was hard pressed to demonstrate that there might be links between this man, XXXXX, and the two drug dealers XXXXX and XXXXX. The claimant offered a variety of explanations in response to the panel's questions on this subject.

He initially replied that he was not certain that this man, XXXXX, could be one of the people who had threatened him, then he stated that the person referred to by his mother might have been one of the people who was in front of his house. When he was questioned later regarding any potential connection between the person who killed his brother and the people who sold drugs in front of his place and who lived four houses from there, he stated that XXXXX, whom his mother mentions in her statement, was one of the people outside when he arrived home. When asked how his mother could have known this, he initially stated that he did not know and then that it was his neighbour who said it. The panel pointed out that it is strange that his mother did not mention any names in her addendum regarding the people involved, and he explained that it was to protect herself since she did not know who it was. The panel pointed out that she had already named XXXXX in her first statement, and so she was not trying to protect herself. He replied that it was indeed because she was scared. The panel asked why she filed a complaint if she would not provide the name of the culprits, and without answering the question, the claimant stated that his mother said that he should not go back there. He later stated that XXXXX also purchased drugs from the two other brothers.

The panel is of the opinion that the claimant is trying to adjust the new facts, namely his brother's death, to his story to accommodate the panel's questions as they arise, and that he repeatedly changed his explanation regarding the possible links between XXXXX and the people who attacked him. He weaves these connections as the hearing evolves. The panel does not believe that there is a connection between his brother XXXXX death and the two drug dealers who were in front of his house, especially given that the panel does not believe that these two men attacked the claimants and, therefore, that the panel does not believe they exist.

Consequently, the panel is of the opinion that this murder is in no way connected to the motives alleged by the claimant's mother, namely a dispute with a neighbour, or those alleged by the principal claimant, namely problems with drug dealers. The panel is of the opinion, rather, that the claimant used this death to support his own story. This undermines his credibility.
For all these reasons, the panel is of the opinion that the claimants are not credible.

Having analyzed all of the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimants did not establish that they face a "serious possibility" of persecution on one of the Convention grounds should they return to Mexico. He also failed to demonstrate that, on a balance of probabilities, they would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, or a risk to their lives or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, should they return to Mexico.

Consequently, their claims for refugee protection are rejected.
